title: A dollar a night, four owners and a business that kept shrinking
lede: Redbox did not lose to a better kiosk. It won the last round of the video rental business, and then went on renting discs for another decade while the customers left.

chapters.title: A vending machine to bring people to the restaurant
chapters.cap: a day plus tax, the rental price in the 2004 Denver test
chapters.body:
By the company’s own account, Redbox originated in 2002 inside McDonald’s Ventures, which was looking for ways to bring more customers to the restaurants. The first idea was broader than films: “a variety of automated convenience options, including fully automated ‘convenience store’ kiosks.” New-release DVD rental was the one customers liked. The same fact sheet dates the start to “an initial launch of 12 kiosks in 2002.”[^1]

In June 2004 the trade press reported that McDonald’s was putting the machines in 104 restaurants around Denver, after a smaller test in fewer than 20 locations in Washington, D.C. and Las Vegas. A rental cost **$1 a day** plus tax and the machines took only credit cards.[^2] In 2005 the test was extended to more than 800 restaurants in five more markets.[^1]

By April 2006 the Associated Press counted 750 machines in McDonald’s restaurants, each about the size of a soda machine and holding 500 discs, and 75 more in grocery stores. Redbox’s head of marketing said its share of all DVD rentals in Denver was “in the low- to mid-teens.”[^3]

pull.text: We think we’re providing a new model for the industry that is going to be difficult for the traditional retailers to compete against.
pull.who: Greg Waring, Redbox vice president of marketing, to the Associated Press, Apr 30, 2006[^3]

chapters.title: The coin-counting company buys it in three steps
chapters.cap: paid by Coinstar in February 2009 for the part of Redbox it did not yet own
chapters.body:
Coinstar, which ran coin-counting machines in supermarkets, invested **$20.0M** for 47.3% of Redbox in December 2005. It paid a further $12.0M a year later, when Redbox met agreed targets, without increasing its share.[^4] McDonald’s kept the majority, and Coinstar expected its share of Redbox’s losses for 2006 to be $4M to $5M.[^3]

On January 18, 2008 Coinstar exercised an option, paid $5.1M and went to 51.0%, and began consolidating Redbox in its accounts.[^5] That February it agreed with Walmart to expand the kiosks in Walmart stores, and by the end of the year there were more than 3,200 there.[^5][^6] The whole network went from 13,700 DVD kiosks at the end of 2008 to 22,400 a year later.[^6][^8]

On February 26, 2009 Coinstar bought the rest from GetAMovie Inc. and the other minority holders (Redbox’s own history describes the seller as McDonald’s) for **$162.4M**: $113.9M in cash and $48.5M in Coinstar shares.[^7][^1] The four payments come to $199.5M (derived).

chapters.title: Hollywood tries a 28-day delay
chapters.cap: the wait for new Warner, Universal and Fox titles agreed in 2010
chapters.body:
A new release for a dollar a night was a problem for the studios, which sold the same disc for many times that. By early 2009 Redbox had sued Universal Studios Home Entertainment over new distribution terms; a year later it had separate complaints against Universal and 20th Century Fox, whose terms would have kept titles out of the kiosks for 30 to 45 days after release.[^6][^7]

Other studios chose to supply it. On July 17, 2009 Redbox signed a licence with Sony under which it expected to pay about $487.0M over the term.[^7] On February 12, 2010 it settled with Warner: Redbox would get the discs **28 days** after they went on sale and dropped its lawsuit. The agreements signed during 2010 with Warner, Universal and Fox all carried the 28-day window.[^7][^8]

It did not slow the growth. Redbox revenue was $773.4M in 2009, $1,159.7M in 2010 and $1,561.6M in 2011, the year it added video games and raised the DVD price to $1.20.[^9] In June 2012 it paid NCR $100.0M for that company’s DVD kiosk business, about 6,200 active machines, which it replaced with its own or removed.[^10]

chapters.title: Forty-four thousand kiosks and nowhere left to put one
chapters.cap: kiosks in 36,400 locations at the end of 2013
chapters.body:
At the end of 2013 there were about **44,000** kiosks in 36,400 locations, in every state, Puerto Rico and Canada. Revenue that year was $1,974.5M, on 775.7 million rentals.[^11] Coinstar changed its name to Outerwall that year. The network had stopped growing: it had added 8,300 kiosks in 2012 and added 300 in 2013.[^11]

The answer to streaming was a joint venture, Redbox Instant by Verizon, agreed in 2012 and launched commercially on March 14, 2013. Redbox withdrew on October 20, 2014, “due primarily to a lower than anticipated subscriber base.”[^11][^12] In January 2015 it decided to shut down in Canada as well.[^12]

In December 2014 the DVD price rose by 30 cents to $1.50 a day.[^12] Revenue per rental went up, and rentals went down: 717.1 million in 2014 and 587.6 million in 2015, a fall of 18.1% in one year. Revenue for 2015 was $1,760.9M.[^13] The annual report’s phrase for it was a “secular decline in the physical rental market.”[^13]

chapters.title: Private, then public again with a going-concern warning
chapters.cap: enterprise value of the 2016 buyout of Outerwall, Redbox’s parent, including net debt
chapters.body:
On July 25, 2016 Outerwall agreed to be bought by funds managed by affiliates of Apollo Global Management for $52.00 a share in cash, about **$1.6 billion** including net debt. The tender offer was paid on September 27, 2016.[^14][^15] Redbox, Coinstar and the rest stopped filing public accounts. We have no kiosk or revenue figures for 2016 to 2018.

Redbox came back to the stock market on October 22, 2021 by merging with a blank-cheque company, Seaport Global Acquisition, with Apollo still holding the majority of the votes.[^16][^17] Its first annual report as a listed company showed what the private years had done. Net revenue had gone from $858.4M in 2019 to $546.2M in 2020 and $288.5M in 2021; the kiosk count was down to 38,379; debt outstanding was $325.4M; and the pandemic’s effect on results, with recurring losses, raised “substantial doubt about our ability to continue as a going concern.”[^17]

The company cut 150 jobs in March 2022.[^18] On May 10 it agreed to be acquired by Chicken Soup for the Soul Entertainment, a streaming company that owned Crackle, for 0.087 of a Chicken Soup share per Redbox share.[^19] The deal closed on August 11, 2022.[^20]

chapters.title: Twenty-three months under the last owner
chapters.cap: total liabilities of Chicken Soup for the Soul Entertainment on March 31, 2024
chapters.body:
The merger brought $359.9M of Redbox debt with it. The buyer later wrote that its ability to service that debt had been “predicated on a partial return to pre-COVID levels in the number and cadence of theatrical releases” and on kiosk rentals returning to about a third of 2019 levels. Neither happened. For 2023 it reported a net loss of $623.0M, including $380.8M of impairments, and said the studios had ended their supply agreements because it could not pay their licence fees.[^22]

The network shrank from about 36,000 kiosks at the merger to about 27,000 in the spring of 2024.[^25][^23] On June 11 the controlling shareholder removed every director but the chairman, William Rouhana.[^24] On June 28 the company filed for Chapter 11 in Delaware, listing about $970M of debts against $414M of assets.[^25][^26] Employees had not been paid for weeks and their health cover had lapsed.[^26][^29]

On July 10, 2024 Judge Thomas Horan converted the case to a Chapter 7 liquidation. Variety reported 1,033 employees out of work without severance, and about **24,000** kiosks to be shut down along with the streaming services.[^26]

pull.text: 1,000 people are about to lose their jobs and they’re not even going to be paid for work that they did.
pull.who: Judge Thomas M. Horan, U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware, Jul 10, 2024, as reported by The Wall Street Journal and quoted in Variety[^26]
